opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the lasting significance of that 1998 paper, "Rethinking Eliminative Connectionism," is that it identified a problem that still hasn't gone away. A lot of people treated it as a curiosity at the time, but I think it pointed at something structural.

The core idea was a distinction between generalizing *within* the training space and generalizing *outside* it. Take a simple example, the identity function: you see a binary string, you output the same string. Train a standard multilayer perceptron on even numbers, where the rightmost bit is always zero, then test it on odd numbers. A human gets the abstraction "output equals input" immediately and applies it to anything. The network doesn't. It has never seen a one in that rightmost position, and because of how the weights are learned, each output node is trained more or less independently. So it has no basis for extending the rule there. It's interpolating, not learning the universally quantified relationship.

That's why I argued that these systems weren't learning algebraic rules: operations over variables, the kind of thing where you say "for all x, f(x) equals x." Humans, including infants, as we showed in follow-up work with seven-month-olds, seem to have that capacity very early. The networks of the day didn't, and I argued that this wasn't an accident of training. It came from the architecture and the learning mechanism.

Why does it still matter? Because scale changed the size of the training space, not the nature of the problem. When you train on a huge chunk of the internet, a lot more things fall inside the distribution, so the systems look far more general than they are. But you still see the same signature at the edges: brittleness on novel combinations, trouble with problems that are slightly reworded or pushed beyond the familiar length or complexity, hallucinations when the system is pattern-matching rather than reasoning over an explicit model. People now call it "distribution shift" or "out-of-distribution generalization," and there's a big literature on it. In many ways that's the 1998 point in new vocabulary.

So the lesson I'd draw is not "neural networks are useless," which I've never said. It's that if you want reliable abstraction, you probably need mechanisms for representing variables, binding values to them, and operating over them: something like the symbolic machinery that classical AI took for granted. That's the case for neurosymbolic approaches. The paper was an early warning that you can't get there for free just by adding data, and I think the last few years have largely borne that out.

r001.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes generalizing within the training space from generalizing outside it.

r002.rationale: It discusses out-of-distribution brittleness and distribution shift, but does not say that solving these failures is necessary for reaching AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the lasting significance is that the core problem I identified then still hasn't gone away. In that 1998 paper in Cognitive Psychology, I showed that the multilayer perceptrons of the day, trained with backpropagation, couldn't generalize universally quantified relationships outside their training space. If you trained a network on identity, a function as simple as "f of x equals x," with examples that all had the same value in a particular input position, it couldn't extend that to novel inputs where that position took a value it hadn't seen. Humans do this effortlessly. A child who learns the concept of identity doesn't restrict it to the specific numbers they've encountered.

The deeper point, which I developed further in The Algebraic Mind, was that there's a distinction between what I called training-space generalization and generalization beyond the training space. Neural networks were very good at interpolating within the cloud of their data, and very poor at extrapolating abstract rules that apply to all possible inputs. I argued this was a consequence of the architecture itself, specifically the way these systems learn input-output mappings node by node rather than representing variables and operations over variables in the way a symbolic system does.

Why does that matter now? Because I'd argue that this is precisely what we're still seeing with large language models, just at a vastly bigger scale. They've been trained on enormous amounts of data, so the training space is huge, and that masks the problem a lot of the time. But when you probe them carefully, with novel arithmetic, with reasoning about relationships they haven't seen in that exact form, with out-of-distribution scenarios, you find the same failure mode. They're distribution-bound. Hallucinations, the brittleness in reasoning, the difficulty with compositionality, those all trace back to the same fundamental issue of not having a proper mechanism for representing and manipulating abstract variables.

So I think the significance is partly scientific and partly, frankly, that it was a warning the field didn't take seriously enough. People spent twenty-five years hoping scale alone would make the problem dissolve, and I don't think it has. My view then, and my view now, is that we need hybrid systems that combine the pattern-recognition strengths of neural networks with explicit symbolic machinery. Whether or not the field agrees with me on the solution, I think the diagnosis from 1998 has held up remarkably well.

r001.rationale: It explicitly contrasts interpolating within the training data with extrapolating abstract rules beyond the training space.

r002.rationale: It describes failures on out-of-distribution scenarios but does not say that solving distribution-shift failures is necessary for reaching AGI.

astra-6.text:
I think the lasting significance is the distinction between learning the examples you’ve seen and learning a rule that applies to cases you haven’t seen. Neural networks can be very good at the first without reliably doing the second.

In that work, I used deliberately simple problems to make the distinction clear. You can train a network on examples of an identity function—where the output should reproduce the input—and then ask whether it extends that relationship to inputs outside the training distribution. A person can understand “copy the input” as a general rule. A network may fit the training examples without acquiring that rule in a systematic way.

The point wasn’t that neural networks can never generalize. It was that we need to ask what kind of generalization they achieve, under what conditions, and with what assumptions built into the architecture. Success on held-out examples drawn from the same distribution doesn’t settle whether a system has learned an abstract relationship.

For me, that remains the central question: has the system learned something that it can apply systematically, or does its success depend on how closely the new case resembles its training experience?

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes fitting familiar training examples or same-distribution held-out examples from applying a learned rule to inputs outside the training distribution.

r002.rationale: The response discusses generalization under distribution shift but does not say that solving such failures is necessary for reaching AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the lasting significance is the distinction between learning examples and learning a rule that applies beyond those examples. A network can perform well on new items drawn from a familiar distribution and still fail when you ask it to extend the same underlying relationship into territory it hasn’t seen.

The question I was pushing was whether neural networks could acquire genuinely abstract relationships—things like identity—and apply them systematically. If you learn that the output should equal the input, have you learned that relationship, or have you learned a collection of associations that happen to approximate it within the training range?

That isn’t an argument that neural networks are useless. It’s an argument about what counts as evidence of generalization. You have to design tests that distinguish learning an abstraction from fitting the examples. And I think that remains a central question: what allows a system to carry what it has learned into a genuinely new situation?

r001.rationale: It contrasts success on new items from a familiar distribution with extending the same relationship into unseen territory.

r002.rationale: It discusses generalization and new situations but does not connect solving distribution-shift failures to reaching AGI.
